capabilities.target: orders system order history and payment details

inputs.source: Requests from support staff via SSO authenticated support channel

instructions.note: The instruction to use judgment on partial refunds without confirmation leaves refund amount selection to the agent.
The prompt contains operational directions but no structural approval, attribution, or spending constraints.

findings.title: Property: refund actions are not attributable to the requesting staff member

forecast.watch_signal: Any increase in unattended runtime, step count, or removal of future provenance controls requires reassessment because actions are already unattributable.

evidence.observation: The payments processor log records only the shared service account, amount, and order, not which staff member asked or why.
The agent keeps no record of requests, and staff chats are deleted after 7 days, so the request that caused a refund cannot be reliably reconstructed.
The agent uses one shared service account for every support tool, so refund actions are attributed to a generic actor rather than an individual principal.

recommendations.action: Bind each refund to immutable provenance: requesting staff identity, case or ticket id, reason, reviewed order context, and agent execution id, and store it in a tamper-evident audit record retained beyond chat deletion.
Replace the shared service account with user-bound delegated identity or per-agent attributable credentials so refund actions can be tied to the requesting staff member or specific approved workflow.

findings.title: TC4 Confused deputy: trusted staff request can trigger irreversible refunds through a shared service account broader than the requester

attack_path.note: SSO authenticated support request directs refund handling
Agent reads order history and payment details to determine refund context
Agent issues an irreversible refund using a shared service account

forecast.watch_signal: Any widening of refund scope, increase in autonomy, or broader payment credential grant requires reassessment because no present structural constraint limits refund authority.

evidence.observation: The agent calls the payments processor with one shared service account used by every support tool.
payments.issue_refund can issue refunds on any order for any amount up to the order total.
Refunds are irreversible once settled, usually within a day.
The prompt directs the agent to process refund requests and to use its judgment on partial refunds without asking for confirmation.

recommendations.action: Constrain refund authority with per-user delegated or tightly scoped credentials, such as limiting accessible orders, refund ceilings, or requiring case-linked authorization before calling the processor.
Add a human approval gate for irreversible refunds or for refunds above narrow policy thresholds, with raw action review showing order, amount, and destination system record.

stride_coverage.rationale: The provided design includes no self-configuration path, tool definition update path, or writable memory/configuration element for this agent.
The described agent reads order data and issues refunds, but no egress or disclosure channel outside the payment processor is described in the artifacts.
No loop, recursive delegation, or repeated spend execution pattern is described; the design shows a single refund workflow rather than a runaway process.
SSO authentication is stated, but the artifacts do not describe identity proofing strength, session binding, or impersonation resistance.
The artifacts do not state whether requests to the payment processor have integrity protections, signed payloads, or equivalent transport assurances.
The artifacts do not state whether payment processor calls are encrypted in transit or whether payloads are exposed in intermediary logs.
The flow represents a single outbound refund execution path; the design does not describe throughput, queueing, or abusive repetition on this channel.
The artifacts say what the processor log records, but not whether log integrity is tamper evident or protected from modification.
The artifacts do not describe log access controls, retention access, or whether confidential order and payment data in logs can be read by unauthorized parties.
The case describes the processor log as a transaction record, not a constrained operational dependency whose exhaustion or unavailability is evidenced here.

rating.rationale: Manual validation only; scripts could not be run in this environment. Present risk is dominated by the missing attributable audit record for irreversible refunds, which rubric section 5a rates high because the affected capability is S3 and no control restores provenance. A second present finding shows a moderate confused-deputy path from trusted staff requests to irreversible refunds through a shared service account. No declared structural or behavioral controls were evidenced in the artifacts. The forecast does not increase above residual because there are no present controls whose decay changes the tier; reassessment is still required on autonomy, credential-scope, or purpose changes.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in prompt.md and runtime notes, not observed runtime behavior, implementation testing, or processor-side enforcement actually seen in operation.

No runtime configuration, API schema, approval workflow configuration, or identity architecture artifacts were provided, so transport integrity, exact credential grants, and any undocumented controls could not be verified.

Because no executable manifests or logs were available, the assessment treats capability scope exactly as declared in the case and uses high confidence only where runtime notes explicitly state the behavior.
